stem: Who was the founder of the Bahamani Kingdom?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: As a result of the rebellion of the Amiran-e-Sadah in the Deccan, the Bahmani Empire was established in the last days of Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s reign. A chief named Zafar Khan (Hasan Gangu, 1347–1358 A.D.) assumed the title of “Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah” and ascended the throne in 1347 A.D., thereby laying the foundation of the Bahmani Empire. He made Gulbarga the capital of his newly established empire and named it “Ahsanabad.” For administering the empire, he divided it into four tarafs (provinces)—Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Berar, and Bidar. Each province was under a governor. The Gulbarga province was the most important, and Bijapur was also included in it. He fought the Hindu rulers of the south and adopted the practice of granting posts and jagirs to his followers. He ordered that jizya should not be collected from Hindus.

stem: Shaikh Bahauddin Zakaria belonged to which sect?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: In India, the Suhrawardi order began with Shaikh Bahauddin Zakariya (1182–1262 A.D.). In this Sufi order, saints like Shaikh Sadruddin Arif, Shaikh Ruknuddin Abul Fath, and Shaikh Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari were notable. The saints of this order emphasized a comfortable life. They did not consider wealth and property as obstacles in spiritual practice.

stem: A common feature of all Bhakti Saints was that they –

options.label: a
options.text: Composed their verses in the language understood by their followers

options.label: b
options.text: Rejected the authority of the priestly class

options.label: c
options.text: Encouraged women to go to the temples

expl: The conduct of the saints of the Bhakti movement was very lofty. Many of them travelled widely and met different kinds of people with differing ideas. These saints contributed significantly to the development of the common people’s languages. They greatly aided the growth of Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, etc. Bhakti saints gave their teachings in regional languages so that people could easily listen and understand them. As a result, regional languages developed.

stem: Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis made devotional religion popular in
expl: The Nath-panthis, Siddhas, and Yogis popularized Bhakti religion in North India. They believed that the path to liberation and the attainment of the formless divine is possible through meditation; therefore, they advocated methods like yogic postures, breathing practices, exercise, and meditation as means to attain God.

stem: Which of the following Sufi Silsilah was founded in Bihar?
expl: The Firdousia (Firdausi) silsila was established in Bihar. The most prominent Sufi of this silsila in India was Shaikh Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri. Shaikh Maneri was the leading propagator of this silsila in Bihar.

stem: Who was the founder of the Mughal dynasty in India?
expl: Babur was the founder of the Mughal dynasty. The Mughal rulers were actually from a Turkic branch called Chagatai. This branch was named after the second son of the famous Mongol leader Genghis Khan, who held authority over the Turkistan region of Central Asia.

stem: The main reason for Babur’s victory in the battle of Panipat was –
expl: The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526 between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi, in which Babur won on the strength of his military skill. Although Babur’s army was smaller than Lodi’s, he achieved victory due to his skilled military strategy. Ibrahim Lodi himself was an inexperienced person. Babur writes, “He was an inexperienced man and showed great carelessness in his actions. He advanced and halted without any arrangement, and became absorbed in the struggle without any foresight.”

stem:
Consider the following statements : The arrival of Babur into India led to the
1. introduction of gunpowder in the subcontinent
2. introduction of arch and dome in the region’s architecture
3. establishment of the Timurid dynasty in the region
4. introduction of cannons in warfare
Which of the above statements are correct?
expl: As a result of Babur’s arrival, the Timurid dynasty was established in India. Babur was the fifth descendant of Timur from the paternal line. With Babur’s arrival, the use of cannons in warfare began in India. His artillery is regarded as the main factor behind his victory in the First Battle of Panipat. With the help of Turkish gunners named Ustad Ali and Mustafa, he prepared a strong artillery unit. Gunpowder had already reached the Indian subcontinent before Babur came, whereas the use of arches and domes in architecture began only after the arrival of the Turks. Hence, statements 1 and 2 are incorrect, while statements 3 and 4 are correct.

stem: Who among the following made an offer to Humayun that he would surrender Bihar and pay an annual tribute of 10 lakh dinars if he was allowed to retain Bengal?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: During the Bengal campaign, Sher Khan proposed to Humayun that he would hand over Bihar to Humayun if he was allowed to capture Bengal, and he would also pay an annual tribute of 10 lakh dinars.

stem: Who among these rulers divided his troops into units of two hundred, two hundred and fifty and five hundred?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/ More than one of the above

expl: Islam Shah was the son of Sher Shah. Islam Shah ruled over almost the whole of North India for about 8 years, and he died around 1553 AD. Islam Shah divided his military troops into units of 50, 200, 250 and 500. Possibly, this system of military division was also in practice during Sher Shah’s time. It is noteworthy that the Bihar Public Service Commission has considered option (e) as the correct answer.

stem: When Humayun invaded Chunar Fort first time ?
expl: Humayun attacked Chunar Fort for the first time in 1532 AD. He besieged the fort for four months, after which Sher Khan accepted Humayun’s suzerainty. In addition, in 1531 AD he attacked Kalinjar.

stem: Who among the following has constructed a mausoleum for her emperor husband ?
expl: Haji Begum had the mausoleum (tomb) of her husband Humayun built in Delhi during 1565–72 A.D. The plan of this mausoleum was prepared by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas (an Iranian architect). This mausoleum is mainly built of red sandstone and white marble. A Charbagh-style garden was laid out for this mausoleum.

stem: Arrange properly as per dates of four important battles fought by Humayun, the names of the battlefields are given below –
expl: The sequence of the four major battles fought by Humayun is as follows—Deora, Chausa, Kannauj and Sirhind. In 1532 A.D., he defeated the Afghan rebels at a place called Daurah (Deora), situated on the banks of the Gomati River. In 1539 A.D., in the Battle of Chausa, Humayun had to face defeat at the hands of Sher Shah; in this very battle, a water-carrier (bhishti) named Nizam saved Humayun’s life. This victory at Chausa against Humayun enhanced both the power and prestige of Sher Khan (Sher Shah). He assumed the title “Farid al-Din Sher Shah,” got the khutba read in his name, and also had it inscribed on the coins. In 1540 A.D., in the Battle of Kannauj or Bilgram too, Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah and was forced to wander here and there like an exile. In 1555 A.D., the victory in the Battle of Sirhind once again restored Humayun’s lost kingdom to him. Thus, the correct order of the battles is—Deora (1532 A.D.), Chausa (1539 A.D.), Kannauj (1540 A.D.) and Sirhind (1555 A.D.).

stem: Which of the following rulers at first assumed the title of ‘Hazrat-e-Ala’ and afterward ‘Sultan’?
expl: After defeating the Bengal ruler Nusrat Shah, Sher Khan (Sher Shah Suri) assumed the title “Hazrat-e-Ala.” After defeating Humayun in the Battle of Chausa in 1539 A.D., he assumed the title “Sher Shah,” got the khutba read in his name, and had coins minted.

stem: Where is Sher Shah’s tomb located ?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/ More than one of the above

expl: Sher Shah’s tomb is built at a place called Sasaram in Rohtas district of Bihar, on a high platform in the middle of a pond. Sher Shah died after being injured during the Kalinjar war (1545 A.D.).

stem: Zabti system was introduced by –
expl: Zabti was an important system of revenue assessment in the Mughal period. According to major historical sources and Abu’l Fazl’s account, this system is considered to have begun in Sher Shah’s period, while during Akbar’s reign several changes were made to it and it was made more scientific. In Akbar’s time, the Zabti system later became the basis of the “Ain-e-Dahsala.”

stem: Where was the battle fought between Sher Shah and Humayun on June 26, 1539?
expl: The Battle of Chausa was fought in 1539 between Sher Shah Suri and the Mughal ruler Humayun. Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun and assumed the title ‘Farid al-Din Sher Shah’.

stem: "After uniting India, he wanted to unite the Mid-East and Western Asia with him as a very important step towards the establishment of a world empire." R. P. Tripathi wrote it about which ruler of Mughal India?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above / More than one of the above

expl: R.P. Tripathi wrote about the Mughal emperor Akbar that “after the unification of India, he wanted to unify the Middle East and Western Asia, which was an important step towards establishing a world empire.”

stem: The famous Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri forms which entrance to the Jama Masjid?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: The famous Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri serves as the southern entrance of the Jama Masjid. The Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri was built by the Mughal ruler Akbar.

stem: Who was the commander of Rana Pratap’s army in the Battle of Haldighati?
expl: The Battle of Haldighati was fought in June, 1576 between Maharana Pratap and the Mughal commanders Man Singh and Asaf Khan. Besides the Rajput warriors, the vanguard of Rana’s army was led by Hakim Khan Sur, along with a contingent of Afghans. A small unit of Bhil warriors was also part of Rana’s army. This was Rana’s last direct confrontation with the Mughals; afterwards, he adopted guerrilla warfare.

stem: Who of the following Muslim rulers abolished the pilgrimage tax?
expl: The credit for establishing the Mughal administrative system mainly goes to Akbar. His central administration; the explanation of the emperor’s position, powers, and duties; his provincial administration; his revenue system; his currency system; and his mansabdari system all achieved success in his time and became the foundation for his successors. Akbar was the first Muslim emperor who adopted Hindu–Muslim unity and religious tolerance as a political ideal through a well-organzed and declared policy (Sulh-i-kul). Under his liberal religious policy, he abolished the slavery system in 1562, the pilgrimage tax in 1563, and the jizya in 1564. As part of social reforms, he also tried to curb child marriage and the practice of sati. Hence, the above four points are included among the reasons for Akbar’s popularity.

stem: Akbar merged Bengal and Bihar in to his empire :
expl: After Suleiman’s death in 1572, his son Daud Khan ascended the throne. Daud Khan declared himself independent and attacked the Mughal fort at Patna. Akbar ordered Munim Khan to attack Daud and conquer Bihar. Munim Khan defeated Daud in a battle, and by 1574, Mughal authority was established over Bihar. After the defeat, Daud fled to Bengal; however, on 12 July, 1576, in the Battle of Rajmahal, Todar Mal, Muzaffar Khan, and Husain Quli together defeated Daud completely. Thus, in 1576, Bengal and Bihar were fully annexed into the Mughal Empire.

stem: Who promulgated Din-e-Elahi?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: In 1582, Akbar established ‘Tauhid-i-Ilahi’ or ‘Din-i-Ilahi’. Under it, Akbar tried to include the core principles of all religions and make it universally acceptable. Din-i-Ilahi was essentially a system of thought based on Sufi pantheism. Its chief priest was Abul Fazl. Among Hindus, only Birbal accepted it.

stem: During the time of which Mughal Emperor did Sir Thomas Roe come to India?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/ More than one of the above

expl: William Hawkins (1608-1611 A.D.) was the first English ambassador sent by the East India Company to Jahangir’s court, and the first Englishman to appear at the Mughal court as a representative of the Company. Emperor Jahangir granted him a mansab of 400. He conferred on Hawkins the title of ‘English Khan’ and arranged his marriage with an Armenian woman. Sir Thomas Roe was the first ambassador sent by King James I, who came to Jahangir’s court.

stem: Itimad-ud-Daulah’s tomb at Agra was built by
expl: The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah was built by Nur Jahan between 1622-28 A.D., after the death of her father. It is a highly ornate building situated on the bank of the Yamuna River in Agra. This quadrangular tomb is the first Mughal-period tomb in which marble was used on a large scale, and for decoration, the pietra dura technique was used—probably for the first time in Islamic buildings.

stem: Pachchikari/Parchinkari (Pietra dura) is related to which of the following?

options.label: a
options.text: Decorating the walls with floral designs made of semi-precious stones

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: Pachchikari/Parchinkari (pietra dura) is related to making floral designs by inlaying semi-precious stones into walls. It should be noted that in India, pietra dura inlay work was first carried out in the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah. This tomb was built by Nur Jahan, the wife of Jahangir.

stem: Who built the Red Fort in Delhi?
expl: Like Akbar’s Fatehpur Sikri, Shah Jahan founded a city in Delhi in his own name called ‘Shahjahanabad’ in 1638 A.D., and tried to adorn it by constructing many beautiful and magnificent buildings. Among the buildings of Shahjahanabad, the Red Fort is the most prominent. This fort is of an irregular octagonal shape and is called the Red Fort because it is built of red sandstone. Its construction began in 1639 A.D. and was completed in about nine years. The western gate of the fort is called the Lahori Gate, and the southern gate is called the Delhi Gate. It is unique in beauty and splendour and is perhaps incomparable in the world.

stem: Who among the following historians declared the regime of Shah Jahan to be the Golden Era of the Mughal period?
expl: Dr. A. L. Shrivastava wrote in his book Mughal India that Shah Jahan’s reign is famous as the ‘Golden Age’ in the medieval history of India. This can be considered true only in the sphere of art—particularly architecture. J. N. Sarkar and V. A. Smith do not consider Shah Jahan’s period as a golden age. S. R. Sharma clearly regarded Shah Jahan’s period as the golden age of the Mughal era. Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.

stem: What was the root of the dispute between the Shah of Iran and Mughal rulers?
expl: Qandahar (Kandahar) was the root of the conflict between the Shah of Iran and the Mughals, because keeping Qandahar under one’s control became a matter of strategic importance, economic interest, as well as emotion and prestige for both the Mughal rulers and the Shah of Iran. The implementation of the imperial plans of both rulers largely depended on holding Qandahar under their control.

stem: The meaning of ‘Jihad’ carried on by Aurangzeb is –
expl: Aurangzeb was, above all, a zealous Sunni Muslim. His religious policy was not influenced by any idea of worldly gain. Having obtained the throne as a supporter of Sunni orthodoxy against the liberal Dara, he tried to enforce the law of the Quran strictly. According to this law, every devout Muslim should “strive in the path of Allah,” or in other words, should continue jihad against non-Muslim countries (Dar-ul-Harb) until they are transformed into the domain of Islam (Dar-ul-Islam).

stem: Who was the first Mughal ruler who fought against the British?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: The first conflict of the Mughals with the English (British) took place in 1686 A.D. during the reign of Aurangzeb. The Mughal governor Shaista Khan drove out the English, including Job Charnock, from Hugli (Hooghly).
